entries.title: C++ Memory Model, Lifetime, and Ownership
entries.detail:
Studied the C++ memory model from a programmer's perspective, focusing on object lifetime and ownership rather than syntax.

Covered:
- Stack vs heap and automatic storage duration.
- Difference between an object's scope and its lifetime.
- Constructor and destructor behavior, including reverse destruction order.
- How new allocates an object dynamically and how delete destroys and frees it.
- Why returning a pointer or reference to a local object creates a dangling pointer/reference.
- Difference between Foo, Foo*, and Foo&:
  - Foo represents an object/value.
  - Foo* stores an address and does not inherently imply ownership.
  - Foo& is an alias to an existing object.
- RAII: tying resource lifetime to the lifetime of an owning object.
- unique_ptr and exclusive ownership.
- Moving a unique_ptr transfers ownership instead of copying it.
- raw pointers obtained from unique_ptr are non-owning observers and can become dangling.
- shared_ptr and reference-counted shared ownership.
- std::move does not move or destroy an object by itself; it enables move semantics.
- Copy constructor vs move constructor.
- A moved-from object still exists and its destructor still runs.

entries.detail:

Description / What Happened
Studied how CPU caches affect real program performance and why memory access patterns can make two O(n) algorithms perform very differently. Explored cache organization, locality, cache misses, hardware prefetching, and memory latency, then validated the concepts through sequential, strided, and random-access benchmarks using chrono and Cachegrind.
Covered

- Cache lines, sets, ways, tags, and associativity
- Address mapping: tag | index | offset
- Direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully associative caches
- Spatial locality and temporal locality
- Compulsory, capacity, and conflict misses
- Memory latency and cache miss costs
- Sequential vs random memory access
- Stride access patterns: 1, 2, 4, 16, 64
- Cache-line utilization
- Hardware prefetching and predictable access patterns
- Working sets, eviction, and cache capacity
- Blocking / tiling for improved locality
- Stack and heap data sharing the same data-cache hierarchy
- vector object vs dynamically allocated vector buffer
- Large-array performance benchmarking with chrono
- Comparing ns/access across sequential, strided, and random access
- perf stat and WSL hardware PMU limitations
- Cachegrind cache simulation
- Reading I refs, I1 misses, LLi misses, D refs, D1 misses, LLd misses, and miss rates
- Experimental observation that stride-1 reuses most of each cache line, while stride-16 and stride-64 approach one cache-line miss per useful array access
- Why absolute miss count and miss probability per useful access are different metrics

entries.title: Urgent Production Hotfix and Cross-Team Ownership
entries.detail:
What Happened
Today I was assigned an urgent production issue that was blocking data from being persisted and reflected in my manager’s manager-level dashboard. My manager trusted me with full ownership of the hotfix, from investigating the root cause and implementing the fix to representing our team while coordinating with QA, DevOps, and other stakeholders to move the PR through the release process.
What made this particularly meaningful was the urgency and level of responsibility. A change would normally take more than two weeks to reach production, but because this issue was blocking important reporting, we had to bring the fix through review, validation, deployment, and production verification within the same day.
The technical issue itself involved multiple layers: fixing malformed LLM JSON handling, improving validation and retry behavior, diagnosing an unexpected AI Core OAuth 429 rate-limit problem, and correcting the concurrency model so OAuth tokens could be safely shared and cached across requests. I also had to make sure the solution was clean, well-tested, Sonar-compliant, and safe enough for an expedited production release.
The biggest takeaway was not only the technical work, but being trusted to own a high-impact production issue end to end. I had to make decisions quickly, communicate clearly with senior engineers and cross-functional teams, respond to review feedback, and remain accountable for the final production outcome. It gave me a much better understanding of what production ownership looks like when the issue is urgent and visible to senior stakeholders.

entries.title: Concurrency Fundamentals
entries.detail:
[[image:/uploads/pasted-7551e045e5e5.png|Pasted image]]

Built a complete mental model of basic concurrency in C++, starting from race conditions and critical sections, then moving through mutexes, atomics, CAS, contention, and deadlocks. Explored why ordinary x++ is unsafe across threads, how atomic read-modify-write operations differ, how CAS retry loops work, and how contention affects synchronization. Finished with a practical benchmark comparing a plain counter, a mutex-protected counter, and an atomic counter.
Covered
- Race conditions and data races
- Critical sections
- Why ordinary x++ is conceptually load → add → store
- Lost updates caused by thread interleaving
- std::mutex
- Mutex ownership, blocking, and waiting
- std::lock_guard and RAII-based unlocking
- Atomic operations and std::atomic
- Atomic read-modify-write operations
- Difference between mutex synchronization and atomic operations
- Atomicity vs thread preemption/context switching
- Hardware implementations of atomic operations
- Load-exclusive / store-exclusive
- Exclusive reservations and retry loops
- Compare-And-Swap / Compare-Exchange (CAS)
- expected and desired semantics in CAS
- CAS failure and retry behavior
- compare_exchange_weak vs compare_exchange_strong
- Spurious failure
- Why weak CAS is useful inside retry loops
- Contention on shared atomic variables
- CAS retries under high contention
- Deadlock and circular wait
- Consistent lock ordering as a deadlock-avoidance technique
- Counter experiment with 8 threads:
  - Plain int: incorrect result due to data race
  - mutex + int: correct result through serialized critical sections
  - atomic<int>: correct result through atomic increments
- Why benchmark results do not imply that atomics are universally faster than mutexes
- Importance of considering contention when evaluating synchronization performance

entries.title: False Sharing
entries.detail:
Cache line ping-pong
[[image:/uploads/pasted-25ebb755b797.png|Pasted image]]
Alignas optimization
[[image:/uploads/pasted-265acbe524c9.png|Pasted image]]
Studied false sharing as a cache-coherence performance problem. Learned why two threads modifying completely different variables can still interfere when those variables share the same cache line. Traced the resulting cache-line invalidation and ownership ping-pong between CPU cores, then verified the effect experimentally by comparing adjacent atomics against cache-line-aligned atomics using alignas(64).
Covered
- False sharing
- Cache coherence at cache-line granularity
- Why different variables can still interfere
- Cache-line ownership and invalidation
- Cache-line ping-pong between CPU cores
- Read-read sharing vs write-induced coherence traffic
- Why one writer can affect another core reading a different variable
- False sharing as a performance issue rather than a correctness issue
- Why false sharing does not require threads to access the same variable
- Cache-line alignment and padding
- alignas(64)
- Difference between aligning a whole struct and aligning individual members
- Struct layout, member offsets, and compiler-inserted padding
- Benchmarking two adjacent atomic<long> counters
- Benchmark result before alignment: approximately 2.57 s
- Benchmark result after separating counters onto different cache lines: approximately 0.66 s
- Observed speedup of roughly 4×
- Why cache-line separation removes unnecessary coherence traffic

entries.detail:
False Sharing experiment

entries.title: C++ Memory Ordering and SPSC Ring Buffer
entries.detail:
[[image:/uploads/pasted-71be9d74d2fd.png|Pasted image]]
Studied the C++ memory model from atomicity through ordering, visibility, happens-before, relaxed ordering, release/acquire, and sequential consistency. Applied these concepts to build and reason about a lock-free SPSC ring buffer, including safe publication of non-atomic data, slot reuse, modification order, local producer/consumer state, and false-sharing avoidance. Finished by benchmarking the SPSC queue against `std::queue + mutex`.

Covered

- Atomicity vs ordering vs visibility
- `sequenced-before`
- `synchronizes-with`
- `happens-before`
- Data race vs logical race / stale observation
- Why atomic objects can be race-free without providing cross-thread synchronization
- `std::memory_order_relaxed`
- Per-atomic modification order
- Why relaxed operations preserve atomicity but not synchronization
- `std::memory_order_release`
- `std::memory_order_acquire`
- Safe publication pattern with release/acquire
- Why plain non-atomic payload data can still be race-free
- Release publishes operations sequenced before it
- Acquire protects operations sequenced after it
- Why reversing publish-before-data order breaks correctness
- `std::memory_order_seq_cst`
- Single global total order for sequentially consistent operations
- Why `r1 = 0, r2 = 0` is forbidden under `seq_cst` but allowed under `relaxed`
- Difference between program order and cross-thread visibility
- Relaxed atomic operations participating inside a larger happens-before chain
- SPSC ring-buffer invariants
- One producer owning the write side
- One consumer owning the read side
- Local non-atomic producer and consumer indices
- Atomic published indices
- `write_index` as producer-to-consumer publication
- `read_index` as consumer-to-producer slot-reuse publication
- Release/acquire synchronization in both directions
- Why ring-buffer slots can remain plain non-atomic memory
- Why SPSC correctness breaks with multiple producers
- Need for atomic slot reservation in MPSC designs
- False sharing between `write_index` and `read_index`
- Cache-line separation with `alignas(64)`
- Why weaker memory ordering does not remove atomic or coherence cost
- `seq_cst` vs acquire/release performance considerations
- Benchmark design and interpretation
- `std::queue + mutex` benchmark:
    - ~29.6M messages/sec
    - ~33.82 ns/message
- SPSC ring buffer benchmark:
    - ~79.0M messages/sec
    - ~12.66 ns/message
- SPSC achieved approximately **2.67× higher throughput**
- Why the benchmark does not isolate mutex cost alone
- Why checksum validation matters in concurrent benchmarks

entries.title: std::vector Internals and Performance Reasoning
entries.detail:
Studied the internal memory model of std::vector, including size, capacity, allocation, growth, reallocation, and pointer invalidation. Connected vector layout to CPU cache behavior and analyzed when contiguous storage can outperform pointer-based data structures despite less favorable insertion complexity.
Covered

- Reallocation process: allocate → move/copy → destroy → free old storage
- Pointer, reference, and iterator invalidation after reallocation
- Geometric capacity growth
- Why geometric growth gives amortized O(1) push_back()
- Why linear +1 capacity growth leads to amortized O(N) insertion
- resize() shrinking size without necessarily shrinking capacity
- std::vector vs linked-list performance beyond Big-O
- Spatial locality and contiguous memory
- Hardware prefetching and cache-line utilization
- Pointer chasing and cache-miss costs
- Workload-driven data-structure selection
- Traversal frequency vs insertion frequency
- Element size and cache behavior
- Pointer/reference stability as a design constraint

- vector<unique_ptr<T>> as an indirection-based stable-address design
- Trade-off between stable addresses and cache locality

entries.title: Ubuntu Dual-Boot & Native Performance Benchmarking Setup
entries.detail:
Description / What Happened

Set up Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS as a dual-boot environment alongside Windows to create a native Linux development and benchmarking environment for C++/systems work. Prepared the disk safely, installed Ubuntu on a dedicated ~110 GiB partition, verified the Linux environment, and validated access to Intel hardware performance counters using `perf`.


Covered


- Decrypted BitLocker-protected Windows volumes before repartitioning.
- Recreated the secondary Windows partition and reserved ~110 GiB for Ubuntu.
- Created a UEFI/GPT Ubuntu installation USB using Rufus.
- Installed Ubuntu with manual partitioning while preserving Windows and the existing EFI partition.
- Verified the disk layout using `lsblk` and `parted`.
- Installed the native C++ toolchain with `build-essential`.
- Compiled and ran a native C++ benchmark.
- Configured and tested Linux `perf`.
- Diagnosed `perf_event_paranoid=4` permission restrictions.
- Collected software counters including context switches, CPU migrations, and page faults.
- Collected hardware PMU counters including cycles, instructions, branches, and branch misses.
- Identified Intel i5-12500H hybrid topology:
    - CPUs `0–7`: P-core logical CPUs.
    - CPUs `8–15`: E-cores.
- Used `taskset` to pin benchmarks to a P-core for more reproducible results.
- Observed approximately **3.49 IPC** on the pinned benchmark.
- Established a development workflow using VS Code alongside terminal-based GCC/Clang, CMake, GDB, and `perf`.

entries.title: Aether Vector vs List Locality Experiment
entries.detail:
[[image:/uploads/pasted-df91aa2d4ddf.png|Pasted image]]Description

Added a focused Aether benchmark comparing sequential traversal of `std::vector<Event>` and `std::list<Event>`. The goal was to measure how memory layout affects real execution time even when both traversals are asymptotically `O(N)`.


Covered

- Created `bench/vector_vs_list.cpp`
- Generated the same 1,000,000 synthetic `Event` objects in:
    - `std::vector<Event>`
    - `std::list<Event>`
- Used the same traversal workload for both containers:
    - `checksum += event.order_id`
- Compiled with GCC using `O3 -std=c++20`
- Ran the benchmark five times on Ubuntu bare metal
- Verified identical checksums for correctness
- Recorded average traversal time:
    - `std::vector<Event>`: ~`2.096 ms`
    - `std::list<Event>`: ~`4.588 ms`
- Measured `std::list` at approximately `2.19x` slower than `std::vector`
- Observed relatively low run-to-run variance
- Connected the result to:
    - contiguous memory layout
    - spatial locality
    - cache-line utilization
    - hardware prefetching
    - pointer chasing
    - dependent memory loads
    - allocation layout
    - larger list-node footprint
    - potential TLB pressure
- Documented the experiment in `docs/vector_vs_list.md`
- Established the principle that identical Big-O complexity does not imply similar hardware performance
- Discussed bottleneck dominance: if per-event CPU computation becomes much more expensive, the relative vector-vs-list gap should shrink

    - `push_back(const Event&)`
    - `erase(Node*)`
- Simplified erase logic using two independent invariants:
    - update previous side or `head`
    - update next side or `tail`
- Current implementation limitation:
    - no destructor for deleting remaining nodes
    - no copy/move semantics
    - intentionally out of scope for the exercise
- `std::list` conceptual node layout
- Larger per-element footprint from link pointers
- Separate-node allocation overhead
- Memory fragmentation considerations
- Poorer spatial locality compared with `std::vector`
- Cache-line utilization differences
- Hardware prefetching advantages of contiguous traversal
- Pointer chasing as a dependency chain:
    - load current node
    - read `next`
    - only then know the next address
- Reduced memory-level parallelism in linked-list traversal
- TLB fundamentals:
    - virtual-page to physical-page translation cache
    - TLB miss vs page fault
- Why scattered linked-list nodes can increase TLB pressure
- Translation reuse within contiguous pages
- TLB working-set size and eviction
- TLB thrashing when repeatedly cycling through more pages than the TLB can hold
- Why sequential pages are not automatically fewer TLB misses if every page is touched only once
- Importance of reuse patterns rather than page order alone
- Performance reasoning beyond Big-O
- Why `O(N)` vector traversal can be much faster than `O(N)` list traversal
- Why `O(1)` list insertion does not automatically make lists preferable
- Workload frequency as a data-structure selection criterion
- Reference stability as a genuine linked-list advantage
- Bottleneck dominance:
    - memory layout matters most when memory access is dominant
    - relative vector/list differences shrink when heavy CPU computation dominates

entries.title: Binary Heap, std::priority_queue, and Scheduling
entries.detail:
Description

Studied binary heap internals, implemented a max-heap manually using `std::vector<int>`, and learned how `std::priority_queue` maps workload requirements to heap-based scheduling. Focused on array-based heap representation, sift-up/sift-down invariants, comparator semantics, min-heaps, deterministic tie-breaking, and choosing between heap, sorting, and top-k strategies.


Covered


- Binary heap as a complete binary tree
- Array representation of a heap
- Parent/child index relationships:
    - `left = 2 * i + 1`
    - `right = 2 * i + 2`
    - `parent = (i - 1) / 2`
- Max-heap invariant:
    - parent value is greater than or equal to children
- Heap does not require globally sorted order
- `top()` complexity: `O(1)`
- `push()` complexity: `O(log N)`
- `pop()` complexity: `O(log N)`
- Heap height: `O(log N)`
- Push process:
    - append at end
    - compare with parent
    - swap upward
    - continue until heap invariant is restored
- Pop process:
    - save root
    - move last element to root
    - `pop_back()`
    - choose the larger child
    - sift downward until invariant is restored
- Why sift-down must swap with the larger child in a max-heap
- Why `erase(begin())` should not be used for heap root removal
- Implemented a mini max-heap using `std::vector<int>`
- Avoided fake sentinel values for missing children
- Avoided unnecessary bit tricks in index arithmetic
- Operator-precedence pitfalls in expressions involving shifts
- Importance of updating the current index after each heap swap
- Single-element heap edge case
- `std::priority_queue` as a container adaptor
- Default underlying storage:
    - `std::vector<T>`
- Why vector is well suited for heap storage:
    - random access
    - `push_back`
    - `pop_back`
    - contiguous layout
- Default `std::priority_queue` behavior as a max-heap
- Min-heap construction using a reversed comparator
- Comparator semantics:
    - returning `true` means the first element has lower priority
- Custom scheduling structure using:
    - timestamp
    - sequence number
    - event
- Deterministic ordering using `(timestamp, seq)`
- Why equal-priority elements do not have stable ordering by default
- Encoding tie-breaking explicitly into the comparator
- Dynamic scheduling:
    - continuously insert events
    - repeatedly execute earliest event
    - heap is a strong fit
- Static batch processing:
    - if all events are known upfront
    - `vector + sort` may be simpler and more cache-friendly
- Top-k reasoning:
    - full sort is unnecessary when only a small number of smallest elements are needed
    - repeated linear scans can be valid when `k` is very small
    - bounded max-heap of size `k` gives `O(N log k)`
    - `std::nth_element` as an average `O(N)` top-k alternative
- Data structure choice based on workload rather than Big-O alone

entries.title: std::map, std::set, and Ordered Data Structures
entries.detail:
Description

Studied ordered tree-based containers at a conceptual level, focusing on balanced BST behavior, `std::map`, `std::set`, ordered queries, and the hardware cost of pointer-based tree structures. Compared balanced trees with sorted contiguous storage and reasoned about when dynamic ordered updates justify the extra cache and allocation overhead.


Covered


- Binary Search Tree invariant:
    - left subtree keys `< node.key`
    - right subtree keys `> node.key`
- BST lookup cost as a function of tree height
- Why a plain BST can degenerate into a linked-list-like structure
- Degenerate BST lookup degrading from `O(log N)` to `O(N)`
- Balanced BST goal:
    - keep height `O(log N)`
    - preserve `O(log N)` lookup, insertion, and erase
- `std::map<Key, Value>` as an ordered associative container
- `std::map` properties:
    - unique keys
    - keys maintained in sorted order
    - `find` — `O(log N)`
    - `insert` — `O(log N)`
    - `erase` — `O(log N)`
- `std::set<T>` as an ordered unique-key container
- Difference between `map` and `set`:
    - `map` stores key + associated value
    - `set` stores only the key
- Ordered iteration
- `lower_bound(x)`:
    - first key `>= x`
- `upper_bound(x)`:
    - first key `> x`
- Minimum and maximum key access
- Why ordered structures naturally support range and boundary queries
- Conceptual tree-node layout:
    - parent pointer
    - left pointer
    - right pointer
    - balancing metadata
    - key
    - value
- Hardware costs of tree-based containers:
    - pointer chasing
    - dependent memory loads
    - branch decisions at each level
    - separate node allocations
    - larger per-element footprint
    - weaker cache locality
    - potentially higher TLB pressure
- Comparison with sorted `std::vector`
- Why sorted vector binary search can outperform `std::map` lookup despite both being `O(log N)`
- Advantages of sorted vector:
    - contiguous storage
    - compact representation
    - no per-node allocation
    - better cache-line utilization
    - smaller working set
- Binary search still has branch-prediction challenges and non-sequential access
- Sorted vector update cost:
    - search position `O(log N)`
    - insert/erase requires shifting elements
    - overall `O(N)`
- `std::map` dynamic-update advantage:
    - maintains order after every insert/erase
    - update operations remain `O(log N)`
- Why trees are useful for workloads with:
    - frequent inserts
    - frequent erases
    - continuous ordered queries
    - minimum/maximum queries
    - `lower_bound` / `upper_bound`
- Why `std::set<Key>` is semantically preferable to `std::map<Key, bool>` for pure membership
- Data-model correctness before micro-optimization
- Choosing between tree and contiguous storage based on update frequency vs lookup/traversal performance

entries.title: Hash Tables and std::unordered_map
entries.detail:
Description

Studied hash-table internals and the performance characteristics of `std::unordered_map`, focusing on exact-key lookup, collision handling, load factor, rehashing, and why average `O(1)` complexity does not automatically imply low or predictable latency.

Covered

- Hash-table mental model:
    - key
    - hash function
    - bucket/index
    - entry lookup
- Average lookup complexity: `O(1)`
- Worst-case lookup complexity: `O(N)`
- Why poor hash distribution can collapse performance
- Hash functions and bucket mapping
- Collision handling at a conceptual level
- Separate chaining:
    - multiple entries associated with the same bucket
    - pointer chasing
    - separate allocations
    - weaker cache locality
- Open addressing:
    - entries stored directly in a table
    - probing on collision
    - better locality potential
- Linear probing mental model
- Why open-addressed tables often benefit from contiguous storage
- Load factor:
    - `elements / buckets`
- Why high load factor can increase:
    - collisions
    - probe/search length
    - memory accesses
    - lookup latency
- Trade-off between:
    - lower load factor and more memory
    - higher load factor and more collision cost
- `std::unordered_map` API:
    - `size()`
    - `bucket_count()`
    - `load_factor()`
    - `max_load_factor()`
    - `reserve()`
    - `rehash()`
- Difference between `reserve()` and `rehash()`
- `reserve(N)` prepares capacity based on expected element count
- `rehash(N)` directly requests a minimum bucket-count target
- Rehashing cost:
    - allocate new bucket structure
    - redistribute existing entries
    - `O(N)` work
- Why pre-reserving can reduce runtime rehash spikes
- Why predictable-latency systems should care about rehashing
- Why over-reserving can increase:
    - memory footprint
    - cache working set
    - TLB pressure
- `max_load_factor()` as a collision/memory trade-off control
- Why lower load factor can improve average lookup behavior
- Why it does not guarantee fixed lookup latency
- Why `std::unordered_map` should not be assumed to use open addressing
- Why `O(1)` does not mean “one CPU operation”
- Real hash lookup path can include:
    - hash computation
    - random-ish bucket access
    - cache miss
    - collision handling
    - additional memory access
- Comparison with sorted `std::vector`
- Why binary search on a small contiguous dataset can outperform a hash table
- Big-O scaling vs real constant factors
- Small working-set effects
- Exact-key lookup as a natural hash-table workload
- Why frequent `find`, `insert`, and `erase` make hash tables a natural candidate
- Why sorted order is unnecessary for `order_id → Order`
- Why Aether should benchmark `std::unordered_map` instead of assuming it is optimal
- Performance factors to benchmark:
    - hashing cost
    - collision behavior
    - load factor
    - cache misses
    - memory layout
    - allocation behavior
    - rehash spikes

entries.title: Linux Non-blocking I/O + epoll
entries.detail:
Description

Covered


- Reviewed blocking `recv()` and thread-per-connection limitations
- Learned `O_NONBLOCK` and `EAGAIN` / `EWOULDBLOCK`

    - `epoll_create1()`

entries.title: Database Storage: From Hardware to Records
entries.detail:
Description

Covered the physical foundations of a disk-oriented DBMS: how relational data becomes bytes, records, blocks, and files, and why query performance depends heavily on storage layout and I/O behavior rather than CPU speed alone.

Covered

- Memory hierarchy: registers, cache, RAM, disk
- HDD structure: platter, track, sector, cylinder, read/write head, actuator arm
- Disk access cost: seek time + rotational delay + transfer time
- Random vs sequential I/O
- Block as the unit of disk transfer
- Data item → field → record → block → file
- Fixed-length vs variable-length fields and records
- Record headers and field boundaries
- Spanned vs unspanned records
- Physical address vs logical Record ID
- Block/file organization
- Record insertion, deletion, deleted slots, and free space
- Why physical clustering of related records improves range-query performance

entries.title: Buffer Pool and Page Management
entries.detail:
Description

Studied how a DBMS uses the buffer pool to reduce expensive disk I/O, how pages are tracked and replaced in memory, and how techniques such as prefetching and scan sharing improve query execution efficiency.

Covered

- Buffer pool, pages, blocks, and frames
- Buffer hits and buffer misses
- Page table and page-to-frame mapping
- Dirty vs clean pages
- Prefetching and CPU/I/O overlap
- Scan sharing across concurrent queries
- Page eviction and victim selection
- Least Recently Used (LRU)
- CLOCK replacement policy and reference bits
- Sequential flooding
- Limitations of recency-based replacement
- Priority hints using query execution context
